backlog.working_title: The Day a City Drowned in Molasses
backlog.premise: Boston, 15 January 1919: a 50-ft storage tank holding about 2.3 million US gallons of molasses bursts. A brown wave reported at up to 25 ft high and about 35 mph floods the North End.
hooks: This city was hit by a wave of molasses.
Twenty-one people died in a flood of something sweet.
The warm January day that turned a sticky tank into a killer.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a brown wave tearing down a city street
OH NO! rivets popping, the tank groaning on an unusually warm day
WHOA! the molasses thickened as it cooled, trapping rescuers and victims; the harbor stayed brown for months
key_visual_moments: Tank bursting, rivets firing like bullets
Rescuers wading waist-deep at dusk as it sets
research_sources: Sharp, Kim et al., APS Division of Fluid Dynamics 2016 (cooling viscosity analysis)
Boston Public Library / Massachusetts Historical Society archives
factual_caveats: 21 deaths and ~150 injured are the commonly cited figures; wave height and speed are contemporary estimates
Treat victims respectfully: no comedic beats about deaths
backlog.notes: Needs a new viscous-fluid effect and a 1919 street set; highest technical risk.

backlog.working_title: The Warship That Sank Before It Could Fight
backlog.premise: Stockholm, 10 August 1628: the royal warship Vasa sails on her maiden voyage before a crowd, heels over in a light gust and sinks within about 1,300 m.
hooks: They spent years building this warship. It sank on its first voyage.
The most powerful warship in Sweden lasted twenty minutes.
A stability test failed. They launched it anyway.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a magnificent warship tipping over in calm water
OH NO! water pouring through open gunports
WHOA! raised almost intact in 1961 and now in a museum
key_visual_moments: The heel and water through gunports
The ship rising from the seabed 333 years later
factual_caveats: Death toll is uncertain (often given as 30-50)
Stability explanations simplified: top-heavy, narrow hull, too little ballast

backlog.working_title: The Glass That Survives a Hammer but Explodes From a Tiny Snap
backlog.premise: Prince Rupert's drops: molten glass dripped into water forms a tadpole whose head resists hammer blows, because its surface is locked in compression, while snapping the thin tail releases the internal tension and the whole drop bursts.
hooks: A hammer can't break this glass. But snapping its tail can.
This glass laughs at a hammer and dies from a pinch.
Why does this tiny glass bomb explode?
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a hammer bouncing off glass
OH NO! a tiny snap at the tail
WHOA! the explosion races through the glass faster than sound in air
key_visual_moments: The crack front racing up the tail
Cutaway: compression skin around a tense core
research_sources: Aben et al., Applied Physics Letters (2017)
factual_caveats: Crack speed is roughly 1.5-1.9 km/s in reported high-speed studies; check exact values before scripting
Do not encourage viewers to make drops at home without safety warnings

backlog.working_title: The Man Who Refused to Believe a Nuclear Attack Warning
backlog.premise: 26 September 1983: at the Serpukhov-15 bunker, Lt. Col. Stanislav Petrov's early-warning system reports US missile launches. He judges it a false alarm and does not pass it up the chain as an attack.
hooks: His computer said nuclear missiles were coming. He didn't believe it.
One man had minutes to decide if the world would end.
The screen said LAUNCH. He said: wait.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! sirens and a LAUNCH warning
OH NO! more missiles appear on screen, minutes tick away
WHOA! sunlight reflecting off clouds had fooled the satellite
key_visual_moments: Red LAUNCH banner in a dark bunker
The satellite and the sunlit clouds
research_sources: David E. Hoffman, The Dead Hand (2009)
Coverage of the 2013 Dresden Peace Prize
factual_caveats: How decisive his single choice was is debated by historians
Avoid inventing dialogue; mark dramatization

backlog.working_title: The Ancient Temple Doors That Opened Without Anyone Touching Them
backlog.premise: Hero of Alexandria (1st century AD) described doors that open when a fire is lit on an altar: heated air pushes water into a bucket whose weight turns the door posts, and they close when the fire dies.
hooks: Nearly 2,000 years ago, someone designed automatic doors.
They lit a fire. The temple doors opened by themselves.
This ancient magic trick was pure physics.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! doors opening untouched
OH NO! the crowd believes it is a god
WHOA! a hidden machine of air, water and rope below the floor
key_visual_moments: X-ray cutaway to the hidden mechanism
Fire dying and the doors closing
research_sources: A. G. Drachmann, The Mechanical Technology of Greek and Roman Antiquity
factual_caveats: Hero DESCRIBED the mechanism; installation in an actual temple is not established
Label the reconstruction on screen

backlog.working_title: The Lake That Released an Invisible Killer
backlog.premise: Lake Nyos, Cameroon, 21 August 1986: a sudden limnic eruption released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide that flowed down the valleys and suffocated about 1,700 people and thousands of cattle.
hooks: The lake didn't flood. It released something nobody could see.
A silent cloud rolled out of this lake in the night.
Why did a peaceful lake kill 1,700 people in one night?
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a calm lake suddenly foaming
OH NO! an invisible cloud flowing downhill in the dark
WHOA! gas dissolved in deep water, like a shaken soda; now pipes vent it safely
key_visual_moments: Visualized CO2 flowing down valleys (clearly marked as visualization)
environments: Lake Nyos crater valley at night and day
factual_caveats: About 1,746 deaths is the commonly cited figure
Tragedy: no comedy; show respect for victims
Gas volume estimates vary

backlog.working_title: The Chess Robot That Fooled the World
backlog.premise: 1770: Wolfgang von Kempelen presents the Mechanical Turk, a chess-playing automaton that tours Europe and America for decades. The secret was a human chess master hidden inside.
hooks: This machine beat humans at chess. Except it wasn't really thinking.
For 84 years, this robot fooled the world.
How did a machine from 1770 play chess?
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a mechanical Turk making a chess move
OH NO! skeptics try to expose it and fail
WHOA! the sliding-seat trick that hid a person inside
key_visual_moments: Cutaway: the hidden operator sliding as doors open
research_sources: Gerald M. Levitt, The Turk, Chess Automaton (2000)
factual_caveats: Famous games against Napoleon and Franklin are reported but details are uncertain
Destroyed by fire in Philadelphia, 1854

backlog.premise: 1901: sponge divers off Antikythera recover a corroded lump from a Roman-era shipwreck. CT scans revealed a geared bronze device that modeled the sky and predicted eclipses.
hooks: Divers found a lump of metal that turned out to be an ancient astronomical computer.
This rock is hiding 2,000-year-old gears.
Nobody built anything like it again for over a thousand years.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! gears inside a sea-worn rock
OH NO! it sat ignored for decades
WHOA! a hand-cranked model of the cosmos predicting eclipses
factual_caveats: Date of the device is debated (roughly 2nd-1st century BC)
Not a 'computer' in the modern sense: an analog calculator; say so

backlog.working_title: How Three Astronauts Survived a Broken Spaceship
backlog.premise: April 1970: an oxygen tank explodes aboard Apollo 13 on the way to the Moon. The crew use the lunar module as a lifeboat and improvise a carbon-dioxide filter fix to get home.
hooks: Their spaceship broke on the way to the Moon. Nobody could come rescue them.
Houston, we've had a problem.
They fixed a spaceship with tape and a sock.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a bang and venting gas in deep space
OH NO! power, heat and air running out
WHOA! a square filter forced into a round hole and a safe splashdown
key_visual_moments: Explosion venting from the service module
research_sources: Jim Lovell & Jeffrey Kluger, Lost Moon (1994)
factual_caveats: The famous line was 'Houston, we've had a problem'
Avoid copying the 1995 film's look or dialogue
backlog.notes: Space set is new work; strong category test for 'survival'.

backlog.working_title: The Tiny Shrimp That Punches Like a Bullet
backlog.premise: The peacock mantis shrimp strikes so fast (about 23 m/s, with accelerations reported over 10,000 g) that it creates cavitation bubbles which collapse with a flash of heat and a second impact.
hooks: This tiny animal punches so fast it creates collapsing bubbles.
This shrimp hits its prey twice with one punch.
The fastest punch in the ocean boils the water.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a shrimp smashing a snail shell
OH NO! the crab doesn't stand a chance
WHOA! the bubble collapse is a second punch
factual_caveats: 'Like a bullet' compares ACCELERATION, not speed; be precise
Species: Odontodactylus scyllarus
backlog.notes: Needs a creature design in the pebble-folk spirit.

backlog.working_title: The Soldiers Who Couldn't Stop an Army of Emus
backlog.premise: November-December 1932, Western Australia: soldiers with Lewis machine guns are sent to cull about 20,000 emus damaging wheat farms. The birds scatter, the guns jam, and the operation largely fails.
hooks: Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to fight birds.
The birds won.
A war against emus. Guess who lost.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! soldiers aiming machine guns at birds
OH NO! the emus split up and run
WHOA! the operation was called off; the emus kept the wheat
key_visual_moments: A truck chasing emus over rough ground
Soldiers' faces as the emus vanish
research_sources: Murray Johnson, 'Feathered foes', Journal of Australian Studies (2006)
factual_caveats: Kill counts vary by report
No graphic violence; keep it comedic and factual

backlog.working_title: The Tiny Animal That Can Survive Outer Space
backlog.premise: Tardigrades in a dried 'tun' state survived exposure to space vacuum and, in some cases, solar ultraviolet radiation on the 2007 FOTON-M3 mission.
hooks: This microscopic creature can survive exposure to the vacuum of space.
This animal went to space without a spacesuit.
How does a water bear survive almost anything?
emotional_arc: WHAT?! a tiny animal on a spacecraft's exterior
OH NO! vacuum, cold, radiation
WHOA! it dries itself into a tun and wakes up with water
factual_caveats: Survival in space was limited, especially with full solar UV
Not indestructible; hydrated tardigrades are fragile

backlog.working_title: The Passenger Jet That Ran Out of Fuel in Midair
backlog.premise: 23 July 1983: Air Canada Flight 143, a new Boeing 767, runs out of fuel at 41,000 ft after a fuelling miscalculation between pounds and kilograms. The crew glide it to a former air base at Gimli.
hooks: Both engines stopped. And there were 69 people aboard.
A jet ran out of fuel because of a math mistake.
The pilot had one advantage: he flew gliders.
emotional_arc: WHAT?! silence as both engines stop
OH NO! no power, gliding toward a runway with people on it
WHOA! a sideslip landing, and no one died
research_sources: Transportation Safety Board of Canada references
factual_caveats: 61 passengers + 8 crew = 69 aboard; minor injuries only
Units mix-up details must be explained accurately

backlog.working_title: How People Made Ice in the Desert Before Electricity
backlog.premise: Persian yakhchāls: on winter nights water froze in shaded shallow pools by radiating heat to the clear sky; the ice was stored through summer under thick domes of insulating mud-brick mortar.
hooks: No electricity. No refrigerator. Yet they had ice in the desert.
Summer in the desert, and this dome is full of ice.
How do you make ice without a freezer?
emotional_arc: WHAT?! ice in desert heat
OH NO! how could it survive summer?
WHOA! the night sky itself was the freezer
key_visual_moments: The giant cone dome at sunset
Cutaway: insulation and the ice pit
factual_caveats: Exact origins and early dates are uncertain; surviving examples are a few centuries old
Radiative cooling explanation must be clear and correct

backlog.working_title: What If Earth Suddenly Stopped Spinning?
backlog.premise: Assume Earth's crust stopped rotating instantly while the atmosphere and oceans kept moving (stated assumption). At the equator the ground moves at about 465 m/s; everything not fixed would keep going.
hooks: Imagine the ground suddenly stopped moving beneath you.
Earth stops spinning. Here's the first second.
What happens if the planet hits the brakes?
emotional_arc: WHAT?! the world stops
OH NO! winds and oceans keep going east at supersonic speed
WHOA! over time the oceans move to the poles and a day lasts a year
key_visual_moments: Air and water sweeping across continents
research_sources: NASA Earth science explainers on rotation
W. Fraczek, ESRI (2007) ocean redistribution analysis
factual_caveats: Clearly HYPOTHETICAL; physically impossible to stop instantly
Results depend on stated assumptions; say so on screen
Avoid graphic depictions of casualties
